prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of neutral atoms brought the measurement of time to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B007) first and I move to optical lattice clocks (B015) as a single-part prize. This is a change of preferred configuration, and the reason is scientific as much as procedural. The chair's first question asks what nature told us through the lattice clock that we did not know, which was my own objection in round 1, so I owe an answer. The magic-wavelength condition is a genuine physical idea: a particular trapping wavelength at which the light shift of the two clock states cancels, so that many neutral atoms can be held in a lattice and read out without a perturbation that limits the measurement. It is not a refinement of the comb (2005) or of single-ion control (2012), which solved different problems. What it produced is not only a better clock. Millimetre-scale gravitational redshift resolved within one atomic sample is a direct laboratory test of general relativity in a regime no other instrument reaches, and the many-body effects seen inside the clock (spin exchange, SU(N) physics) are new physics about interacting atoms that nobody planned. Reproduction at the 1e-18 level by several independent laboratories, which Stefan Kroll and Eva Lindroth both stress, means the systematics have been tested by people other than the inventors. That is the maturity I ask for before the question of who deserves credit even arises. And on credit, all eight of us name Katori and Ye, which is the cleanest attribution on the list. IceCube remains for me the more exciting discovery, but I cannot defend a three-name division in a citation to the same standard, and I will not set the cleaner case aside to protect my first instinct.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still that lattice clocks are an invention plus record performance, not an unexpected finding, and that the dark-matter and constant-drift searches so far give bounds, not detections. A third precision-metrology prize in two decades after 2005 and 2012 needs the citation to name the lattice scheme and not just precision, otherwise it reads as an increment. The redefinition of the second has not happened and I would keep it out of the citation, as Mark Pearce proposes. A second weakness is the split between Katori's concept and first strontium clock and Ye's accuracy, stability and many-body results; Eva Olsson is right that the invention and the later record should be kept distinct in how we describe the two. Competing ion-clock lines at comparable uncertainty and the many groups at PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN are not credited, and the citation should not imply a single origin of the clock family. Finally, a prize that favours a precision measurement over IceCube's observed phenomenon leaves open the question I started with, whether we reward discoveries of new phenomena or capabilities, and I do not regard that as closed.

responses.point: Stefan places the lattice clock first as a new measurement capability with the cleanest two-name attribution, and asks that the citation not imply a single origin for the clock family.
responses.response: Stefan, your answer to my round-1 question is what moved me. The null results on constants and dark matter are bounds, I agree, but millimetre-resolved redshift and the many-body physics inside the clock are things the instrument has actually shown, not promised. I accept your wording point and would not attach a two-part configuration with atom interferometry or IceCube, because the three-person limit would force us into the credit problems of those entries on top of a clean pair. I remain a little uneasy that the strongest payoffs are still prospective, but that is a reason to word the citation around the invention and its demonstrated performance, which you have already proposed.

responses.point: Mark moved from IceCube first to the lattice clock, keeps IceCube as his first alternative, and argues that source identification need not delay the neutrino discovery while three names are hard to defend.
responses.response: Mark, we started from the same first choice and we now end in the same place for the same reason: I cannot write a citation that divides IceCube's credit among Halzen, Karle and Spiering, with Olsson's Halzen and Karle pair as the live alternative, and defend it against the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage. I agree that the redefinition of the second should stay out of the citation; if the General Conference slips, the physics case does not change. I still hold that the diffuse-flux discovery stands without KM3NeT or Baikal-GVD confirmation of sources, so B007 is a serious candidate for a later year if the names can be settled, and I would not see it as a lesser result.

responses.point: Eva moved B015 to the top because Katori's magic-wavelength lattice is the original invention and Ye's JILA systems demonstrated the 1e-18 realization, and asks whether Ye's role is invention or later realization.
responses.response: Eva, I think your framing is right and the citation should carry it: Katori proposed the scheme and built the first strontium lattice clock, and Ye's group took it to the accuracy and stability frontier and added the many-body regime. Ye's work is not merely later polish, because it showed that the idea survives at 1e-18 with large atom numbers, which is what turns a proposal into a clock. I would therefore keep the pair and word the citation as invention and realization. On IceCube, you are right that my three names are historically more complete than your two, and that completeness has a price in the lineage we leave out; that is part of why I let it go this round. I also note that Spiering's role in the AMANDA and discovery analysis is the one point I could not settle.

responses.point: Eva Lindroth argues that the magic-wavelength lattice is distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, that independent reproduction shows maturity, and that the ion-clock line is a strong rival.
responses.response: Eva, as the atomic physicist you are best placed to settle the novelty point, and your account (neutral atoms in a lattice, thousands interrogated at once, a regime of many-atom clocks) persuades me that it is a step different in kind from the comb and the single ion. Your remark about competing Al+ ion clocks is the fair caveat, and it argues for naming the lattice scheme in the citation rather than claiming the whole field of optical clocks. I also accept your correction of my round-1 reading of your IceCube view: your caution about thin source evidence is a reason to prefer the diffuse-flux wording, and I would keep that if B007 returns.

uncertainties: Whether the committee is satisfied that the magic-wavelength condition is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes; my own answer rests on my recollection of the physics and on the atomic physicists' testimony, not on an independent check.
How to split credit in wording between Katori's concept and first strontium clock and Ye's accuracy and many-body results without implying a single origin of the clock family.
Whether Spiering belongs in a future IceCube prize, or whether Halzen and Karle suffice, and whether the neutrino discovery should have been recognised first.
Whether source-population evidence from IceCube alone will be adequate or independent confirmation will be needed; I have not checked source significances against external sources.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal. My work in string theory, dark energy and dark bubble cosmology is distant from atomic clocks and neutrino astronomy, and I have no recorded personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or any other credited name. Eva Lindroth's and Stefan Kroll's disclosed connections to atomic physics and to JILA do not change my view of the evidence.
